GARP Coding Guide
ECON 600 · Problem Set 3 · Optional coding exercise

Testing GARP on real choices

A step-by-step guide to checking whether each subject in the Data_LZ experiment makes choices that some utility function could explain. It follows the algorithm sketched in Tutorial 6.

How this exercise works

  • Use any programming language you like.
  • Use AI as much as you want, but not a frontier model. Pick a lighter one, such as the free Gemini app (Flash-Lite) or Claude Haiku.
  • A weaker model forces you to explain the algorithm clearly. That skill is the point of the exercise. Honour code applies.

1The data

Data_LZ has 82 subjects. Each subject faced the same 22 budget lines in two goods, x and y, and picked one bundle on each. One row is one choice. Subject IDs are labels, not a count from 1 to 82: they run from 105 to 2306 with gaps.

SubjectObservationx_choseny_chosenx_maxy_max
105125.8825.8810034.92
105210402080
1053303061.5758.5

x_max and y_max are where the budget line hits each axis. The line through them is

x / x_max + y / y_max = 1

So you can treat income as 1 and prices as p_x = 1/x_max and p_y = 1/y_max. Then the cost of any bundle (x, y) at the prices of budget i is

cost_i(x, y) = x / x_max_i + y / y_max_i

Every comparison below comes down to this cost.

2Comparing two choices

Take two observations i and j from the same subject. When the subject chose bundle i, was bundle j also affordable?

  • j cost strictly less than what was spent at i: the subject passed up j while it was cheaper, so i is strictly revealed preferred to j, written i ≻ j.
  • j cost exactly the same: i is weakly revealed preferred to j, written i ≿ j.
  • j was too expensive: we learn nothing. This does not mean j ≿ i. That would need its own check on budget j.

In symbols, with spent_i = cost_i(bundle i):

i ≿ j   if   cost_i(bundle j) ≤ spent_i
i ≻ j   if   cost_i(bundle j) < spent_i
Pitfall: compare with what was spent, not with the full budget

The chosen bundles are rounded, so they are rarely exactly on the budget line. For subject 105, spending ranges from 0.9992 to 1.0001. In theory a subject spends the whole budget, so "cheaper than the full budget" and "cheaper than what was spent" are the same test. Once bundles are off the line, they differ. If you compare against the full budget (cost ≤ 1 with income normalised to 1) instead of against actual spending, rounding creates violations that aren't real.

For example, subject 105 chose the same bundle (26.23, 26.23) on budgets 8 and 9. It costs 0.99992 under both, a hair inside each line. The budget-line rule gives 8 ≻ 9 and 9 ≻ 8, which is a GARP violation between two identical choices.

Comparing against spent_i fixes this, and it also makes every bundle automatically weakly preferred to itself. That was the first fix suggested in the tutorial (set the diagonal to 1). The second fix, allowing some slack, comes back in the extensions.

3Store every comparison

Run the comparison for every ordered pair (i, j) of one subject, which is 22 × 22 comparisons. Store the results in two matrices:

  • W, where W[i][j] = 1 if i ≿ j
  • S, where S[i][j] = 1 if i ≻ j

Every strict link is also a weak one, so S[i][j] = 1 implies W[i][j] = 1. The diagonal of W is all 1s and the diagonal of S is all 0s. You could instead use one matrix with codes 0, 1 and 2, but two matrices keep the next step simpler.

Think of W as a directed graph: one node per observation, with an arrow i → j whenever i ≿ j. The rest of the algorithm searches this graph.

4What a violation looks like

GARP fails when the choices chain back to where they started with at least one strict link along the way:

a ≿ b ≻ c ≿ … ≿ a

In graph terms, this is a cycle of W arrows where at least one arrow is also in S. A cycle made only of weak links is fine: it just says the bundles are all equally good. So the task is to find every cycle and check each one for a strict link.

5Find the cycles: search, check, merge

This is the algorithm from the tutorial. Depth-first search (DFS) explores the graph by following arrows as deep as possible, then backing up one step and trying the next branch. When the search returns to its starting node, it has found a cycle.

  1. Pick a starting node s.
  2. Run a DFS from s along the arrows of W. Each time the search comes back to s, you have a cycle.
  3. Look up every link of that cycle in S. If any link is strict, stop: GARP is violated, and the cycle is your evidence.
  4. If every link is weak, the nodes on the cycle are all indifferent. Merge them into one node that keeps every arrow in and out of its members. Then go back to step 2, starting from the merged node.
  5. When the search from s finds no more cycles, s is cleared: no violation passes through it. Remove it from the graph and pick a new start.
  6. If every node gets removed, the subject satisfies GARP.

Two details are easy to miss:

  • Links into a merged node. An arrow e → (abd) stands for several original links: e → a, e → b and e → d. It is strict if any of them is strict. The tutorial's reminder was to recheck all of them, for example a ≻ c or b ≻ c or d ≻ c.
  • Links inside a merged node. Members of a merged node all lie on one weak cycle. So a strict link between two members, such as a ≻ d, is already a violation, even if the search reached d through b.

6Run it on every subject

Loop over the 82 subjects, build W and S for each, and run step 5. Report which subjects pass, and for each one that fails, the cycle that breaks GARP.

7Extensions

How bad is the violation?

A failed test treats a tiny slip and a wild inconsistency the same. Two ways to measure the size:

  • Cycle length. A two-step cycle (i ≻ j ≻ i) contradicts itself directly. A long chain is a subtler inconsistency.
  • Money pump index. Ask how much budget you would have to take away to break each link. For the link i ≻ j, shrink budget i parallel to itself until bundle j stops being strictly cheaper. That amount is spent_i − cost_i(bundle j), the ε from the tutorial. An arbitrageur could extract this much money from the subject each time around the cycle.
MPI(cycle) = Σ over links (spent_i − cost_i(next bundle))
             ─────────────────────────────────────────────
                     Σ over links spent_i

Fill a matrix with these ε values, one per strict link, and you can score every cycle. A subject with several cycles could report the largest or the average MPI. Note that some violations are tiny: subject 206 has a cycle with an MPI below 0.001, which is within rounding of the data.

Shrinking every budget at once

The money pump shrinks budgets one cycle at a time. Afriat's efficiency index applies the same idea to every budget at once. Pick a factor e between 0 and 1 and count a link only if the other bundle fits inside the shrunken budget:

i ≿ j   if   cost_i(bundle j) ≤ e × spent_i
i ≻ j   if   cost_i(bundle j) < e × spent_i

With e = 1 this is the test from step 2. Lowering e drops the links where the other bundle was only just affordable, so cycles break and more subjects pass.

A subject's efficiency index is the largest e at which they pass. An index of 1 means fully consistent choices. An index of 0.95 means the choices fit some utility function once every budget gives up 5% of its income. How would you find each subject's index? Do the subjects with the lowest index also have the largest money pump?
